parts: A harsh, strong coat protects this breed from adverse weather. This is one of the most important qualities all sheepdogs must possess, as they have to withstand prolonged exposure to both rain and heat.
Because of the abundance and length of its coat, we will look beneath it to assess the characteristics required by the Old English Sheepdog breed standard.
For this reason, it is crucial to use both hands and eyes to examine the dogs properly. Only then will we take the coat into account to complete the assessment.

The general appearance of the Old English Sheepdog is that of a strong, compact, well-angulated and balanced animal. Remember that the Bobtail is a "worker". The breed has inherited and developed great soundness, a characteristic of vital importance.
The ideal Old English Sheepdog should be thickset, muscular, strong and sturdy. Its coat should be harsh and abundant. Texture is more important than quantity.

Height from the withers to the ground should be 24' (60 cm) for males and 22' (56 cm) or more for females. Above all, always remember that the animal's character and balance are more important than size alone.

In proportion, the Old English Sheepdog's body should be as tall as it is long. Its measurement from shoulder to buttocks should be virtually the same as from withers to ground. It should be well muscled, strong, compact, square and balanced. Overall proportions are of great importance.
STANDARD
The skull should be capacious and square in shape.
The orbital bones should be well arched. The head should feel broad, with no angles that detract from its square appearance.
Stop well defined.
Muzzle distinctly long, strong and square. Truncated.
Viewed from the front, the muzzle should be broad and square, with a large, substantial black nose.
The head should be well balanced, substantial and square in appearance.
The teeth should be evenly aligned, meeting perfectly, or with the upper teeth "slightly ahead". They should be large, strong and long, with well-defined spaces between them.

The eyes should be set wide apart and be dark brown or blue. One brown eye and one blue eye (wall eye) is also quite common. Brown eyes should be very dark. Blue, pearl or china eyes are considered typical.

The standard does not mention pigmentation around the eyes, and dogs with little or no pigmentation are perfectly acceptable. However, dogs with good eyelid pigmentation are preferred, as it enhances their beauty.
The ears should be medium-sized, flat and well set on the sides of the head.
Viewed from the front, despite the abundant hair concealing it, we can see the typical features that give the Old English Sheepdog its highly intelligent expression.

The neck is distinctly long and gracefully arched. Its length should be proportionate to create an impression of balance. Bear in mind that both coat markings and exaggerated grooming can affect the visual assessment of the neck's true arch or length.
The shoulder blades and upper arms are equal in length, and the distance from the shoulders to the elbows should be virtually the same as from the elbows to the ground.
The forelegs should be completely straight, with good bone. The elbows should fit close to the body, and the chest should extend well down to the elbows.
The Old English Sheepdog's chest is very broad when viewed from the front. Remember that the forequarters should be angulated, with shoulders narrow at the points.
Feet small and round, with well-arched toes. Pads thick and hard.
The body should preferably be short and very compact. The ribs are well developed and well sprung, with a deep, capacious chest.
The ribcage is not overly broad. This allows the forelegs and shoulders to move freely.

The Old English Sheepdog standard clearly states that, when the dog is standing, the distance from the withers to the ground is slightly less than from the loin to the ground. This difference in height can be seen by drawing an imaginary line from the withers to the loin. The resulting curve makes the Bobtail entirely unique among breeds.
This curve should be gradual. An overly pronounced curve is undesirable, as is one that is deep, abrupt or uneven.
The loin itself is sturdy and gracefully arched.
The tail should not project beyond the body, having been docked during the first days of the animal's life.
The hindquarters should be rounded and muscular, with good angulation to balance the forelegs.
The hocks should be well let down. The rear pasterns should be completely perpendicular to the ground, whatever the viewing angle.
Males should have two apparently normal testicles descended into the scrotum.
THE COAT
We now turn to the vitally important subject of the coat:
The coat should be of good quality, with a harsh texture. It should not be completely straight, but should be free from curls.
A soft or limp coat is faulty.
The undercoat provides waterproof protection in the rain.
The outer coat should feel harsh and wavy to the touch.
The coat should be abundant but not excessive, as this can make the dog appear obese.
The ears should lie close to the head and be moderately coated.
The hair should fall over the neck and muzzle.
The forelegs should be coated all around. The front feet should be densely coated.

As for colour, any shade of grey, blue or bluish colouring tending towards blue merle is acceptable. The body and hindquarters are of a uniform colour, with or without small white markings (socks) at the ends of the limbs. Any shade of brown should be considered objectionable and must never be encouraged. The light and dark areas of the coat should be clearly defined and distinct. White streaks and white patches in the dark areas should be penalised. Bear in mind that a puppy's coat will change in colour, texture and abundance. A somewhat brownish tinge in puppies is common.

The Old English Sheepdog should be presented as naturally as possible, without exaggerated grooming. Excessive grooming may lead a specialist judge to suspect that structural faults are being concealed. For this reason, we stress the importance of consistently using the hands to feel the animal beneath the coat.
Excessive grooming and the use of artificial methods give the Bobtail an unnatural appearance.

Remember that the Old English Sheepdog standard states that the coat's natural texture must be preserved and the dog's best qualities highlighted, without using any additional products or artificial aids.
It is very instructive to look at a Bobtail with a good coat and then at one that has been clipped, to understand everything discussed above.
MOVEMENT
In movement, the dog should appear light yet powerful. It should cover as much ground as possible with the fewest steps. It has an elastic, rolling walk and an agile, swift gallop.
In the ring, we can distinguish three fundamental characteristics of its movement:
* Elastic at the gallop.
* Free and rhythmic when walking and trotting.
* Highly distinctive when ambling.

Note that the Old English Sheepdog may amble at slow speeds. This characteristic is perfectly acceptable. It has a distinctive gait, its ambling or pacing action, resembling a bear's walk, in which the foreleg and hindleg on one side move together, followed by those on the other side. This type of gait is uncommon in other breeds, where it is seen only in puppies and elderly dogs. In the Bobtail, however, it is the usual way of walking.

When watching the dog run towards us, the forelegs should always remain close together; they should neither stray out to the sides nor, still less, cross over. Viewed from behind, even at higher speeds, the legs should remain perfectly vertical from hips to pads.
Greater or lesser speed is not considered a fault. The key is power and balance in movement.
CHARACTER
Finally, we will discuss the character and temperament of the Old English Sheepdog:
* A thoroughly adaptable and intelligent animal.
* Playful, mischievous and always ready for anything.
Aggression, timidity and nervousness are not characteristic of the Bobtail's temperament.
One of the finest qualities of the Bobtail's temperament is its constant readiness for any task, work, game or other activity, always with the best of humour and the greatest enthusiasm.

However, when studying the Old English Sheepdog closely, we must remember that its traditional role is that of a sheepdog that drives and protects livestock. Today, it has turned its herding talents into a remarkable ability to adapt to family life.
Strong, sturdy, intelligent, gentle and kind-hearted.
That is the Old English Sheepdog!!
MAIN FAULTS
Any departure from the above should be considered a fault and penalised according to its severity.
